lines.text: A land of desert caravans and holy cities, of a ruling family and an ocean of oil. This is the story of Saudi Arabia.
Around the start of the common era, the Nabataeans carved great tombs into the sandstone cliffs of Hegra, on the incense roads of Arabia.
By the fifth century, Mecca was a trading town in the western hills, and a shrine of many gods.
Around 570 Muhammad was born there. Muslims believe he received the Quran, and by his death most of Arabia followed Islam.
At the heart of Mecca stood the Kaaba, the stone cube that Muslims everywhere would come to face in prayer.
In 622 Muhammad built his mosque in Medina, the second holiest site in Islam, where he would later be buried.
His move to that oasis city that year, the Hijra, marks the first year of the Islamic calendar.
In 632 he made the pilgrimage to Mecca, and the Hajj that Muslims still make today follows its rites.
Over a thousand years later, in 1727, the Saud family first ruled a state in central Arabia, the root of today's kingdom.
In 1744 Muhammad bin Saud of the Najd made a pact that would bind his house to faith and power.
Allied with the preacher Ibn Abd al-Wahhab, the Al Saud built the first Saudi state at Diriyah, until it was crushed in 1818.
Not far away lay Riyadh, then a mud-walled oasis town, now a capital of millions.
In 1876 Ibn Saud was born. In 1902 he took Riyadh, and went on to unite most of the peninsula.
His son Faisal, born in 1906, would rule as king and modernise the state.
Another son, Salman, born in 1935, would become king in 2015.
In 1938, at Dammam, the drillers finally struck oil in commercial amounts, and everything began to change.
In 1973, under King Faisal, Arab producers cut oil to Israel's backers, and the world learned the power of Saudi oil.
In 1979 armed militants seized the Great Mosque of Mecca, and it took two weeks of fighting to end the siege.
In 1985 Mohammed bin Salman was born, the crown prince who would become the kingdom's most powerful figure.
In 1988 the oil company born of the Dammam find became Saudi Aramco, owned by the state, and one of the most valuable firms on Earth.
In 1990 Iraq invaded Kuwait, and a coalition led by the United States gathered on Saudi soil to drive it out.
In 2016 the crown prince announced Vision 2030, a plan for life beyond oil, with cinemas and tourism opening up.
The next year came Neom, a planned city of the future in the northwest desert.
In June 2018, after decades of campaigning, Saudi women were finally allowed to drive.
That October the journalist Jamal Khashoggi was killed inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul, and the world looked on in anger.
From caravan roads to oil and new cities, Saudi Arabia is still remaking itself.
